summary: Describes common mistakes found in DNS implementations and suggests fixes for them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1536 describes common errors in DNS software that caused unnecessary network traffic. It recommends fixes such as waiting longer before retrying, limiting repeated queries, and caching negative answers.

questions: what is a dns fast retransmission
why do dns resolvers need negative caching
what are common dns implementation errors
subtitle: Common DNS implementation errors that cause unnecessary queries, with fixes proposed in 1993.

tldr.problem: Different DNS implementations interacted in ways that produced large amounts of unnecessary traffic on the NSFnet backbone.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes recurring errors in retransmission, referrals, answers, server-failure detection, caching, name errors, and query formats, then suggests fixes.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 9210.

today: RFC 1536 is Informational, not a standard, and has been updated by RFC 9210. Its examples describe BIND versions and DNS practices discussed in October 1993.

sections.title: Why the Memo Was Written
sections.content:
The authors observed a large increase in Domain Name System (DNS) traffic on the NSFnet backbone. Different implementations and versions interacted in ways that created unnecessary queries. RFC 1536 documents known problems and ways to repair the software.

Where relevant, it points out differences from RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. It also uses BIND versions 4.8.3 and 4.9 as examples of implementation behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: Some DNS software repeated work or handled answers poorly, increasing traffic. The memo describes those behaviors and suggests ways to reduce the extra queries.

sections.title: Retries and Unresponsive Servers
sections.content:
DNS clients may need to retry a query when no response arrives, but retrying too quickly sends duplicate traffic across the network. The RFC recommends estimating round-trip time or choosing a sufficiently long initial timeout, then increasing the wait exponentially. It also recommends limiting retransmissions.

A resolver should try another server when one does not respond and should avoid repeatedly querying a server that appears unavailable. The BIND examples use limits and round-trip estimates; the full-service resolver described in the memo backs off exponentially to a 45-second ceiling.
sections.plainLanguage: If a DNS server does not answer, wait before retrying and increase the wait after each retry. Try other servers and set a limit so the client does not keep asking forever.

sections.title: Referral Loops and Empty Answers
sections.content:
A resolver may follow referrals from one name server to another. A broken configuration can send it back to the same server or around a loop. The RFC recommends limits on referral and canonical name (CNAME) links, checking for self-referring servers, and accepting iterative answers from servers that do not perform recursion. BIND versions discussed in the memo limit chasing to 20 referral links and 8 CNAME translations.

A valid name may have no record of the requested type. In that case, an authoritative NOERROR response with no answer is meaningful and should not trigger endless retries. The memo says BIND does not query one server more than 3 times and recommends an upper limit on retransmissions.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolvers should stop following referrals when they enter a loop or exceed a limit. An authoritative reply with no requested record is an answer, not a reason to repeat the query without end.

sections.title: Caching and Name Errors
sections.content:
A cache leak occurs when a resolver repeats a query even though it has a usable record in its cache. The RFC recommends interpreting time-to-live (TTL) values correctly and using enough cache space to retain records for their specified lifetime.

NXDOMAIN means the queried name does not exist. Resolvers should stop after this answer, and negative caching can prevent repeated queries for the same nonexistent name. The memo also warns that search-list behavior can turn a valid name into several unsuccessful names first. It recommends trying names containing dots as fully qualified domain names before appending a local domain. A secondary server should not answer until it has loaded its zone data.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a cached answer until its TTL expires, and remember negative answers so the same missing name is not queried repeatedly. Try a complete name before adding a local domain suffix.

sections.title: Query Format and Security Notes
sections.content:
Some resolvers send query packets that do not conform to the relevant standards. The RFC says this wastes network traffic and server time, and recommends correcting the resolver or checking packets before sending them.

The Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in the memo. The document focuses on implementation behavior that can cause repeated work, incorrect answers, or excess traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Resolvers should send queries in the defined format. This memo does not discuss security issues; it focuses on implementation errors and their operational effects.
